content: A community morbidity register form is provided as an example and should be adapted to the local context. This form is designed to assist health workers in identifying patients with lymphedema and hydrocele during patient estimation exercises or other morbidity management and disability prevention (MMDP) activities. It can also be used alongside a lymphedema job aid to help community health workers assess the severity of lymphedema. The form includes fields for the health center name, community health worker name, patient demographics (e.g., name, age, sex, village address), date of enrollment, and details about the location and severity of lymphedema or scrotal swelling. It also records the number of acute attacks in the last 30 days and whether the patient is known to the health system. Severity is categorized as mild (lymphedema without folds, potentially reversible overnight), moderate (lymphedema with shallow folds), or severe (lymphedema with skin changes such as mossy lesions, knobs, or deep folds). An individual intake form for community health workers is also provided as an example. This form should be modified to the local context to help health workers assess the status of new lymphedema or suspected hydrocele patients. It includes documentation of key demographic data, findings from patient interviews and physical exams, the presence and location of swelling, lymphedema staging, entry lesions, and a history of acute attacks. Health workers should train patients in the five components of lymphedema management: hygiene, skin and wound care, elevation, exercises, and wearing comfortable shoes. Patients with danger signs (e.g., chest pain, shortness of breath, fever with sweats, unexplained weight loss, jaundice, or rapid swelling) should be referred immediately to a health facility for further evaluation. Scrotal swelling should also be referred to a hospital for diagnosis and potential hydrocele surgery. A follow-up form for community health workers is provided to track the progress of lymphedema patients over time. At each visit, health workers should document the date, the number of acute attacks in the past 30 days, and whether the patient is adhering to recommended lymphedema management practices. Referrals to hospitals should be noted if necessary, and any observations or advice given to the patient should be recorded. The form can be adapted to display one visit per page or used longitudinally, depending on the local program's standard operating procedures. An example reporting framework outlines the flow of MMDP data from community health workers to the national level and from the national level to the World Health Organization (WHO). Reporting should occur at least annually and be integrated with existing health information systems where feasible. Forms are provided for community health workers to report to health centers, for health centers to report to implementation units, and for implementation units to report to the national level. These forms summarize data on the number of lymphedema and hydrocele patients, new cases identified, and patients receiving care. They also track referrals and surgeries performed. National programs are encouraged to report MMDP data annually to the Global Programme to Eliminate Lymphatic Filariasis (GPELF) using the provided reporting forms. These forms include data on known and new cases, care provided, and referrals, ensuring comprehensive tracking and management of lymphedema and hydrocele cases.
